key_insight: This paper shows that AI licenses can be lost or replaced as artifacts move from datasets to models to applications, creating “license laundering” in the supply chain. By tracing over 232,270 chains, the authors reveal that downstream AI releases often fail to preserve upstream legal obligations.
problem_solved: It addresses the lack of evidence on whether dataset and model licenses survive redistribution across AI platforms, and whether obligations are stripped away as artifacts move from Hugging Face to GitHub and beyond.
method: Traced 232,270 dataset → model → application supply-chain chains across major AI platforms.
Measured two forms of license laundering: missing original licenses and replacement with different downstream licenses.
Analyzed how often license obligations fail to propagate through real-world AI artifact reuse.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights a legal and compliance risk in reusing public datasets and models. Teams need stronger license tracking and governance to avoid unintentionally redistributing artifacts without honoring upstream terms.
visual_elements: Supply-chain flow diagram showing dataset → model → application with license labels changing or disappearing.
Stacked bar chart comparing preserved, missing, and replaced licenses across stages.
Warning icon overlays on chain nodes to illustrate laundering points.
Platform logos or nodes for Hugging Face and GitHub to show cross-platform movement.
paper_title: Don't Trust the Label: License Laundering in AI Supply Chains
paper_authors: James Jewitt, Hao Li, Gopi Krishnan Rajbahadur, Bram Adams, Ahmed E. Hassan
